title: Effect of Buried-Interface Preparation for Nb Superconducting Resonators on InP
authors: Logan S. Kusher, Ding Peng, Zihua Zhu, Arunav Bordoloi, Axel Leblanc, Lukas J. Baker, Nichae Adnan, Jacob Issokson, Alvin Wang, Frederik Knudsen, Krishna Dindial, Melissa Mikalsen, Taha Kaleem, Andrei Vrajitoarea, Yingge Du, Patrick J. Strohbeen, Javad Shabani
abstract: Substrate surface preparation is a key step in the fabrication of electronic devices. In III--V semiconductor platforms, e.g. used in HEMTs and lasers, removal of the native substrate oxide is extremely important, where improper removal will negatively affect end-of-line device performance. However, the impact of substrate preparation in hybrid superconductor--semiconductor (S--Sm) systems relevant to quantum information applications remains poorly understood. This study compares three surface preparations for the deposition of sputtered Nb films on InP: (i) no intentional oxide removal (control), (ii) \textit{in-situ} $\mathrm{Ar}^{+}$ milling, and (iii) S-passivation. \textit{In-situ} $\mathrm{Ar}^{+}$ milling reduces the O concentration at the metal--substrate (MS) interface, but also roughens the InP surface, increasing the effective thickness of the Nb--InP interface and promoting O incorporation through extended defects in the Nb film. S-passivation suppresses interfacial O more effectively while preserving a sharper and smoother buried interface. It also yields Nb films with higher superconducting transition temperatures and less structural damage than the $\mathrm{Ar}^{+}$-milled samples. Despite these materials improvements, the microwave response is comparable across the three preparations. At single photon powers, the highest internal quality factors, $Q_i$, are approximately $1.30\times10^{5}$ ($130\mathrm{k}$) for the control resonators, $9.7\times10^{4}$ ($97\mathrm{k}$) for the S-passivated resonators, and $8.4\times10^{4}$ ($84\mathrm{k}$) for the $\mathrm{Ar}^{+}$-milled resonators. These results suggest that the present devices are not primarily limited by dielectric loss at the buried Nb--InP interface.
summary: This paper investigates how different substrate cleaning methods affect superconducting resonators made with Nb on InP. By comparing as-received, Ar+-milled, and S-passivated surfaces, the authors found that while S-passivation improved material quality, the resulting microwave losses were similar across all samples. This suggests that the primary limitation for device performance is likely due to substrate or packaging losses, rather than the buried metal-semiconductor interface itself.
main_problem: The study aims to understand and mitigate microwave loss in hybrid superconductor-semiconductor (S-Sm) systems, focusing specifically on the poorly understood buried metal-substrate (MS) interface.
main_result: While S-passivation improved material quality (higher $T_c$, smoother interface) compared to Ar-milling, the measured internal quality factors ($Q_i$) were comparable across all preparations, suggesting the loss is not primarily due to the buried interface.
method: The researchers compared three substrate preparations (control, Ar+-milled, S-passivation) by measuring microwave resonance responses ($Q_i$) and characterizing the interfaces using ToF-SIMS, AFM, and STEM.
model_or_system: The physical system involves superconducting resonators fabricated using sputtered Niobium (Nb) films deposited on Indium Phosphide (InP) substrates, forming a critical S-Sm junction.
key_observables: Internal quality factor ($Q_i$), normalized impurity ratios (O:In, C:In, S:In), interface width, and surface RMS roughness.
important_parameters: The comparison is made at single photon powers, and the key parameters are the relative performance of the three surface treatments.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the measured microwave loss is not dominated by the dielectric loss at the buried Nb–InP interface, pointing instead to substrate or package losses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the three structural preparations, show ToF-SIMS depth profiles comparing impurity incorporation, and present AFM/STEM images detailing interface morphology and roughness.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of problem identification (poorly understood interface loss) $ightarrow$ experimental comparison of three preparation methods $ightarrow$ detailed material characterization (chemical, structural) $ightarrow$ measurement of microwave response ($Q_i$) $ightarrow$ conclusion that loss is extrinsic to the interface.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses loss mechanisms in superconducting circuits, which is crucial for building quantum devices, by systematically ruling out the interface as the primary loss source.
